old: I live in Sénégal, where “intentional community” often sounds like a strange Western phrase for something people assume human beings already do.
new: I live in Sénégal, where "intentional community" often sounds like a strange Western phrase. Don't human beings already do that?
why: B's reaction as the locals' own question, kept to the published point: something people assume humans already do (B's "are you people not doing that in the West already??" turned it around)

old: This country feels unlike anywhere else I’ve lived. Five times a day, devotional prayers pour into the streets. I find them deeply soothing. Sufi spirituality appears in music, public images, murals, names, and ordinary conversation rather than remaining inside designated spiritual spaces.
new: Sénégal is unlike anywhere else I've lived. Five times a day the prayers pour out into the streets, and I find them so soothing. And Sufism doesn't stay inside designated "spiritual" places here. It's in the music, in the pictures everywhere, in the murals, in the names, in the conversations.
why: A's run-on list; "People are devout in a way I've never seen before" and "praying ... out in the streets" were A's (the published prayers pour into the streets)

old: I also hear people laughing outside for hours. This is the most intensely joking culture I’ve encountered, and I keep wondering whether I’ll ever understand the really complicated jokes in Wolof. Basic conversation is one thing. Knowing why twelve people are suddenly crying with laughter is graduate school.
new: And the humor! People are outside laughing for hours at a time. It's the most joking culture I've ever been in, and I keep wondering if I'll ever understand the really complicated jokes in Wolof. Basic conversation is one thing. But knowing why twelve people are suddenly crying with laughter? That's graduate school.
why: A's "And the humor!"; the published "understand" the jokes (A had "make jokes") and its "twelve people" (A: "a bunch")

old: In the villages and families I’ve spent time around, land, childcare, housing, food, and obligation often pass through extended family and local memory alongside formal systems. Nobody needs to announce a workshop called “Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging.” An aunt has already assigned three people a task.
new: In the villages and families I've spent time around, a lot of what we're trying to "re-invent" with intentional community is just done. Land, childcare, housing, food, obligations, etc. all go through the extended family and local memory, alongside the formal systems. Nobody has to announce a workshop called "Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging." An aunt has already given three people a task.
why: A's "re-invent ... just done"; "with my family here" was A's slip (he stays with a friend's family); the published local memory, formal systems, workshop and aunt back

old: Even in Dakar I found graffiti reading, “Tolerance! Openness! Union! Happiness! Love!” Murals of Sufi leaders appear elsewhere. Spiritual graffiti still surprises me because I grew up expecting urban walls to advertise either a product or somebody’s inability to draw a penis.
new: Even in Dakar, I see things like this spray painted on walls: "Tolerance! Openness! Union! Happiness! Love!" And elsewhere there are murals of Sufi leaders. Spiritual graffiti still surprises me! Where I grew up, a city wall was either selling you a product or showing off somebody's inability to draw a penis.
why: A's "spray painted"; the published "elsewhere" and the product-or-penis expectation (B's "f**k the police" left out)

old: I don’t want to turn this into Sénégal as a surviving communal paradise either. The warmth has hard boundaries, and LGBTQ+ people can pay brutally for crossing them.
new: Not that Sénégal is some communal paradise that survived! The warmth has hard limits, and for LGBTQ+ people who cross them, it can be brutal.
why: A's "it can be a brutal place"; the published stance and limits

old: In March 2026, Sénégal enacted [Law No. 2026-08](https://www.humandignitytrust.org/resources/law-no-2026-08-of-march-27-2026-amending-article-319-of-law-no-65-60-of-july-21-1965/), raising the penalty for consensual same-sex intimacy to five to ten years in prison. The amended article also criminalizes public “apology” for homosexuality and certain financing or support intended to promote it. The law comes within the context of an existing reality of arrests, family rejection, harassment, assault, and mob violence—some say prison actually protects homosexuals from the mob. I don’t want to praise communal belonging while ignoring people who survive that belonging by hiding who they are—or by leaving.
new: In March 2026, Sénégal passed [Law No. 2026-08](https://www.humandignitytrust.org/resources/law-no-2026-08-of-march-27-2026-amending-article-319-of-law-no-65-60-of-july-21-1965/), which raised the penalty for consensual same-sex intimacy to five to ten years in prison. It also makes public "apology" for homosexuality a crime, and certain financing or support meant to promote it. And that's on top of the arrests, rejection by family, harassment, assault and mob violence that were already happening. Some people say that once homosexuals are arrested they're actually protected in jail, because the mob can't get at them. I'm not going to praise communal belonging while ignoring the people who survive it by hiding who they are, or by leaving.
why: A's jail sentence; the law's wording A put in quotation marks is out (the published section doesn't quote it), as are A's "constant" and "endemic"; the published closing stance back

old: A society can be spiritually alive, generous, funny, and intensely communal while still becoming cruel toward people who violate its accepted categories. Community itself isn’t automatically liberating. Everything depends on who is permitted to belong without pretending.
new: So yes, a society can be spiritually alive, generous, funny and super communal. It can also be cruel to people who break its categories. Community isn't automatically freeing, then. It depends on who gets to belong without having to pretend.
why: A's and B's "So"; the published criterion (who may belong without pretending) for their "it depends on the community"

old: The otherwise forgiving social culture has other shadows, too. People may avoid confrontation so thoroughly that everybody knows who stole the sheep and nobody wants to create trouble by saying it aloud.
new: The forgiving social culture has its shadows too. People avoid confrontation so much that everybody knows who stole the sheep, and nobody wants to make a stink by saying it out loud.
why: A's "make a stink"; the published sheep, kept apart from the moringa pods, which A had folded in

old: The older communal patterns are also changing. Young people move toward cities, jobs, phones, imported foods, and the wider world. Men take dangerous sea routes toward Europe. Families that once shared nearly everything become more dependent on cash and individual opportunity.
new: But the old communal ways are changing too. The young people are heading for the cities, for jobs, phones, imported food, the wider world (and some of the men take the dangerous sea route to Europe). Families that used to share nearly everything end up depending more on cash, and on individual opportunity.
why: A's parenthesis for the men; commas for A's "and ... and" chain (Joel's rule); "another world" stays in H2-P6, as published

old: One strange survival of the old communal system is what people call the “Black Tax”: when one person begins earning money, they’re expected to support parents, siblings, cousins, school fees, medical bills, funerals, and whoever else the family is carrying. I understand the instinct behind it. In the ancestral arrangement, nobody succeeded alone. The people who fed, raised, housed, and protected you had a real claim on whatever prosperity later came through you. Sharing wasn’t charity. It was how the whole organism survived.
new: One strange leftover of the old communal system is what people call the "Black Tax." If you make any money at all, you're expected to support your parents, your siblings, school fees, medical bills, funerals, whoever else the family's carrying. I understand the instinct, though. In the ancestral way of doing things, nobody made it alone. The people who fed you, raised you, housed you and protected you had a real claim on whatever you made of yourself later. So sharing was how the whole organism survived. Nobody thought of it as charity.
why: B's "if you make any money at all"; A's "ground zero" and "I used to cringe at this" out; the published list of who is carried, the claim and the organism back; "cousins" goes under his list rule

old: The modern version can become soul-destroying because the obligation survived while much of the communal life supporting it disappeared. The land, labor, childcare, food, and daily belonging are no longer fully shared, but the person earning cash may still be expected to carry everybody. They struggle to build any independence or long-term stability, while the relatives receiving the money remain dependent because the payments don’t create a viable alternative. The ancestral ethic is still alive inside an individualistic cash economy, where it can keep people alive while quietly consuming both sides.
new: Today it can be soul destroying, because the obligation is still there but most of the communal life that held it up is gone. People don't share the land, the work, the childcare, the food and the daily belonging the way they did, but whoever earns the cash can still be expected to carry everybody. They can hardly build any independence or long-term stability. And the relatives who get the money stay dependent, because the payments don't give them any real alternative. The ancestral ethic is still alive, just inside an individualistic cash economy now. It keeps people alive, and it eats away at both sides while it does.
why: B's order; the published survival of the obligation, the viable alternative and both sides back; "quietly" out

old: This is also the boundary problem a money-free commune has to solve. Internal life can be cashless while taxes, hospitals, visas, school fees, family obligations, imported tools, and other outside relationships still arrive denominated in money. The question is not whether to recreate individual wages inside the commune. It is who handles that interface, how much collective cash is kept for it, and how to stop access to outside money from becoming a new status hierarchy.
new: It's also the boundary problem any money-free commune runs into. Life inside can go without cash, but taxes, hospitals, visas, school fees, family obligations, imported tools, etc. all still come with a price in money. And no, that doesn't mean bringing individual wages back inside! It means somebody has to handle all that, and the group has to decide how much shared cash to keep for it. And how do you stop access to outside money from turning into a new status hierarchy?
why: B's question for the hierarchy; A's "as you say" out; the published boundary and wages back

old: Outside work complicates that boundary even before a common purse. It does not only bring cash. It brings another schedule, status system, social world, set of loyalties, and often new consumption expectations. During the first stage, an outside earner should contribute an agreed share, but money cannot buy exemption from ordinary communal work or extra political authority. The group also has to notice when outside jobs are draining the people and skills needed to build shared livelihoods. Otherwise the commune remains a dormitory for the cash economy instead of moving toward a common purse.
new: Outside work complicates that boundary too, and it starts before there's a common purse. Cash is only part of what it brings in. There's another schedule, another status system and social world, other loyalties, and often new habits of consumption. In the first stage, whoever works outside gives the commune an agreed share, but the money can't buy them out of doing their share of the communal work, or buy extra political authority. And the group has to watch for outside jobs draining the people and skills it needs to build shared livelihoods. Otherwise the commune stays a dormitory for the cash economy, and the common purse never happens.
why: B's "whoever is working outside" and "buy their way out of work"; A's "into the common purse" out (the first stage comes before it); the published dormitory back

old: Zapatista communities faced a version of this with migration. Some moved from trying to stop young people from leaving toward negotiated arrangements in which migrants could work elsewhere while retaining defined communal obligations. The conflict between mobility and belonging did not disappear. It became something the community could name and negotiate.
new: Zapatista communities ran into a version of this with migration. Some of them used to try to stop their young people from leaving, and now they negotiate with them instead: migrants can work elsewhere as long as they keep defined obligations to the community. The pull between leaving and belonging didn't go away. But now it's something the community can name and negotiate.
why: A's "used to try to stop ... now ... negotiate"; A's "I've heard" and "given up trying" out

old: Westerners often begin with isolation and try to rebuild tribe. Many Africans begin with inherited communal life and watch parts of it dissolve. Urban Africans interested in intentional community may arrive after feeling alienated from both the city and the tradition they left.
new: Westerners often start out isolated and try to rebuild a tribe. A lot of Africans start out with a communal life they inherited, and watch parts of it fall apart. And urban Africans who get interested in intentional community might come to it feeling alienated from both the city and the tradition they left.
why: A's "a lot of africans ... opposite direction" in the published shape; A's "trying to hold on to it" and "a similar position to a westerner" out

old: That makes this a global conversation rather than a Western lifestyle niche. Living villages still contain knowledge no book can reproduce, but they are living people rather than exhibits. Go respectfully, contribute something, learn the language, and do not arrive expecting a spiritual service package.
new: So this is a global conversation. It's way bigger than some Western lifestyle niche. There's knowledge in the living villages that no book can give you. But they're people, not exhibits! If you go, be respectful, and be ready to contribute and learn the language. Just don't show up expecting a spiritual service package.
why: B's "be respectful ... learn the language" and "Don't go there expecting"; A's "I recommended" out

old: A practical note: my own residency process in Sénégal was inexpensive and straightforward. French and Wolof matter much more than English. The country’s famous ideal of *Teranga*—hospitality—is real in my life: I stay in a friend’s family house, and they refuse rent. That generosity exists beside watchfulness, social conservatism, bureaucracy, and all the ordinary complications of a real country.
new: Oh, and a practical note: getting my residency here was pretty cheap and straightforward. French and Wolof matter a lot more than English. And the country's famous ideal of Teranga (hospitality) is real in my life. I'm staying in a friend's family's house, and they won't let me pay rent! Of course that generosity lives right alongside watchfulness, social conservatism, bureaucracy and all the usual complications of a real country.
why: B's "it was pretty cheap and easy to get residency here" (his own process, as published; A generalized it) and "they won't let me pay rent"; the published watchfulness back
